issues.legal_issue: The statutory power to control exports includes the power to regulate who may participate and to channel exports through selected agencies.
material_facts: A mine owner sought a licence to export manganese ore under a system that restricted exports through quotas and selected categories of exporters.
The export-control order allowed the licensing authority to channel exports through special or specialised agencies or channels.
The statutory scheme empowered the government to prohibit, restrict or otherwise control exports.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the statutory power covered canalisation, including restrictions on the persons permitted to export, and that the provision authorising canalisation was within the government’s rule-making power.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3 of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947, control of exports may extend to persons participating in export trade, and canalisation is one permissible form of that control. The Court relied on Glass Chatons Importers and Users Association v. Union of India, which had upheld the validity of the canalisation provision in the Export Control Order.

predicates.export_control_challenge: A person challenges the legal authority for restrictions imposed on the export of goods.
predicates.exports_are_restricted: The government limits the quantity or circumstances in which goods may be exported.
predicates.exports_are_channelled_through_selected_: The government directs that exports may be conducted through selected agencies or channels.

issues.definition: When an export-control challenge concerns restricted exports or exports channelled through selected agencies, the rule treats canalisation as within the government’s statutory power.

issues.legal_issue: Canalising exports through a state trading agency and excluding new entrants from direct export may be a reasonable restriction on the right to carry on trade when it serves the public interest in reliable, quality-controlled exports and foreign-exchange earnings.
material_facts: There was little domestic demand for the ore, and it was produced mainly for export.

New mine owners without export performance during the selected earlier years were excluded from direct export quotas and could sell their ore only to established exporters or the state trading corporation.
Foreign buyers sought regular supplies of ore of uniform quality, and there had been complaints about supplies not matching samples.
The government sought to maximise foreign-exchange earnings and considered the state trading corporation better placed to advance those objectives.
The appellant did not allege that the established shippers and mine owners included in the export scheme had been improperly selected.
issues.conclusion: The majority held that the canalisation scheme, including the preference for the state trading corporation and the consequent exclusion of new entrants, was a reasonable restriction in the interests of the general public and did not violate the right to carry on trade. Subba Rao J. dissented, concluding that the scheme’s effects on excluded mine owners were unreasonable.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(g) protects the right to carry on trade, subject to reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public under the first part of Article 19(6). Canalisation necessarily entails excluding some groups; the government may select an agency more likely to achieve the purpose of canalisation. The majority concluded that a monopoly or near-monopoly created by these restrictions could be sustained as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(6), without relying on Article 19(6)(ii). Subba Rao J. considered that a state monopoly could not be justified by the specific exception in Article 19(6)(ii) without a law, but assessed the restrictions under the general reasonable-restriction test. He referred to Saghir Ahmad v. State of Uttar Pradesh in discussing the constitutional amendment and the statutory basis for state monopolies.

rule.if: export_control_challenge and little_domestic_market and reliable_uniform_supply_needed and foreign_exchange_earnings_sought and selected_state_agency_better_suited and (newcomers_lack_export_experience or canalisation_excludes_some_traders)

predicates.export_control_challenge: A person challenges export restrictions as an interference with the right to carry on trade.
predicates.little_domestic_market: There is little domestic demand for the goods, leaving producers substantially dependent on export markets.
predicates.reliable_uniform_supply_needed: Foreign buyers need regular supplies of goods meeting consistent quality standards.
predicates.foreign_exchange_earnings_sought: The government seeks to increase the country’s foreign-exchange earnings through exports.
predicates.selected_state_agency_better_suited: The government selects a state trading agency because it considers that agency more likely than other channels to achieve the export-policy objectives.
predicates.newcomers_lack_export_experience: The traders excluded from direct export have no relevant prior export performance.
predicates.canalisation_excludes_some_traders: The export scheme channels trade through selected participants and thereby excludes other traders from direct participation.

issues.definition: When an export-control challenge concerns goods with little domestic market and the government channels exports through an agency considered better suited to secure reliable supplies and foreign-exchange earnings, the majority’s rule treats the restrictions as reasonable even if inexperienced newcomers are excluded.

issues.legal_issue: Can administrative export controls that exclude mine owners from direct export and leave them without a guaranteed purchaser or fair terms impose an unreasonable restriction on their right to carry on trade.
material_facts: The ore had little domestic market, so excluded mine owners depended on established exporters or the state trading corporation as purchasers.
Neither the established exporters nor the corporation was required to purchase any particular quantity from the excluded mine owners.
The excluded mine owners could be left without a buyer or required to accept prices dictated by the available purchasers.
The restrictions progressively reduced private export participation and eventually left the state trading corporation with a virtual monopoly.
No definite rules guaranteed excluded mine owners quotas, purchases, or fair prices.
issues.conclusion: Subba Rao J. concluded that the restrictions destroyed or crippled the trade of mine owners in the appellant’s position and were unreasonable under Article 19(1)(g), although the majority rejected that conclusion.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(g) protects the right to carry on trade, and restrictions must satisfy the general reasonable-restriction requirement in Article 19(6). Article 19(6)(ii) does not itself confer power to create a state monopoly by administrative action; it protects a monopoly created by a valid law. Subba Rao J. considered that an export-canalisation scheme should provide definite safeguards, such as fair allocation and treatment, rather than leave producers dependent on purchasers’ discretion. He discussed Saghir Ahmad v. State of Uttar Pradesh in relation to the constitutional treatment of state monopolies.

rule.if: export_control_challenge and newcomers_excluded and no_guaranteed_purchase and producers_depend_on_purchasers_for_prices and no_definite_fairness_safeguards

predicates.export_control_challenge: A person challenges export restrictions as an interference with the right to carry on trade.
predicates.newcomers_excluded: Producers without prior export performance are excluded from direct participation in export trade.
predicates.no_guaranteed_purchase: The selected exporters or agencies are not required to buy goods from the excluded producers.
predicates.producers_depend_on_purchasers_for_price: The excluded producers have no effective market and must depend on selected purchasers to sell their goods.
predicates.no_definite_fairness_safeguards: The scheme contains no definite safeguards ensuring fair allocation, purchase arrangements, or prices for excluded producers.

issues.definition: When an export-control scheme excludes producers who have no alternative market and provides neither guaranteed purchases nor definite safeguards for fair treatment, Subba Rao J.’s rule treats the restrictions as unreasonable.
